s: Today's episode is a little different, because today is review day.
Instead, we are revisiting all the vocabulary from the last three days.
Tuesday was housing and renting, Wednesday was emotions and character, and Thursday was money and shopping.
Seven phrases about homes, seven deep character words, seven money expressions.
If you studied every day, this is your victory lap.
If you missed a day, this is your rescue boat.
Let's start with Tuesday's housing words.
A home truth is an unpleasant fact about yourself that happens to be true.
My friend once gave me a real home truth.
She said I spend too much money on coffee shops.
It stung, but it was fair.
That's the thing about a home truth.
It hurts because it is honest.
The best advice often starts with a home truth.
And notice, a home truth is personal.
It is about you, not about the world.
When something hits home, it is fully understood and it has a strong effect on you.
His words about poverty really hit home for me.
You can read statistics all day, but one personal story can hit home harder than a hundred numbers.
And a compliment can hit home too, right?
When someone says something kind and you truly feel it, that hits home in the best way.

A household word is a person or thing that everyone knows.
Coca Cola has become a household word globally.
Every culture has its own household words.
Here is a challenge for listeners: think of a household word in your country that nobody abroad would recognize.
And the last housing word: have the time of your life.
We had the time of our lives at the party.
To have the time of your life is to enjoy yourself immensely.
It is such a joyful phrase.
Who had the time of their life this week?
I had the time of my life at the farmers market on Saturday, no joke.
I had the time of my life too, Maya, watching you haggle over tomatoes.
Hey, it was an art form.
Okay, Wednesday's theme was emotions and character, and honestly, these are some of my favorite words of the week.
An approachable person is friendly and easy to talk to.
Her approachable manner made students feel comfortable asking questions.
If people are afraid to talk to you, you are not approachable, and everything gets harder.
Being approachable is a superpower at work.
To feel alarmed is to feel frightened or worried.
The sudden noise left her feeling alarmed.
I was alarmed last night when the fire alarm went off at two in the morning.
I stayed alarmed for a good ten minutes after it stopped.
To appease someone is to calm them down by giving them what they want.
He tried to appease his angry boss with an apology.
Trying to appease people is a useful skill, but there is a limit.
If you always appease everyone, you end up pleasing nobody, including yourself.
Someone who is altruistic shows selfless concern for the well-being of others.
His altruistic actions benefited the entire community.
I think altruistic people make the world work.
Volunteers, donors, the neighbor who shovels your driveway.
Antipathy is a deep seated feeling of dislike.
His antipathy towards modern art was well known.
Lena, let me connect some dots here.
Someone with real antipathy for dishonesty might deliver a harsh home truth.
And an altruistic friend might tell you that home truth kindly, to help you grow.
The words are talking to each other.
An approachable manager might appease an alarmed employee by being honest.

Now, Maya, take us to Thursday.
Let's start with the big one: achieve economic growth.
When a country achieves economic growth, it increases its wealth and prosperity.
Governments aim to achieve economic growth every year.
A country can achieve economic growth while millions still live in abject poverty.
Abject poverty is the state of being extremely poor and without hope.
Growth on paper does not always reach the street.
That's why policy makers try to alleviate debt for struggling families.
To alleviate debt is to make it less severe.
One tool is to allocate funds wisely.
Governments allocate funds for schools, hospitals, roads.
When they allocate funds well, the whole country benefits.
And ordinary people have money words too.
It is the yearly cost of borrowing money.
Always check the APR before taking out a loan.
I learned that the alarmed way.
And what about boost the economy?
Government spending aims to boost the economy.
When leaders spend on jobs and projects, it can boost the economy for everyone.
It can, if they are astute.
An astute leader spots what actually works.
An astute investor reads the market before jumping in.
Astute is one of my favorite words this week.
It means having an ability to accurately assess situations or people.
Be astute with your money, listeners.
To abhor is to intensely dislike something.
She truly abhors any form of injustice.
I also abhor alarm clocks that go off at two in the morning.
Two more from Tuesday I want to rescue: high-rise and hovel.
A high-rise is a tall building with many floors.
They live in a modern high-rise downtown.
And a hovel is the opposite.
They lived in a tiny dilapidated hovel.
The contrast between a high-rise and a hovel tells you a lot about a city.
And the last one: lead a sheltered life.
To lead a sheltered life is to live protected from difficult experiences.
She led a sheltered life, unaware of real world challenges.
One trip, one conversation, and suddenly you understand why people talk about abject poverty the way they do.

So to sum up Thursday: governments try to achieve economic growth, they allocate funds, they alleviate debt, they boost the economy, and the rest of us just check the APR and hope our own little economy achieves growth too.
